q-114999:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{9}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{9}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I \\ 10I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡(e)-{ln}^{10}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

q-49609:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I) \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-15421:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6({e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I) \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-36I \\ 37I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{6x}}{37}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-49967:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3J \\ I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3(-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3I) \\ I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{10}){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2\pi )}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ))}{10}-\frac{{e}^{3(0)}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{6\pi }}{10}-\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{6\pi }-1)\end{aligned}
$$

q-71128:
Note that the length of the altitude $DH$ can be related to the area of $△\,DMA$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot MA
$$

So, to find $DH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{MD}$ and $\overset{\to }{MA}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{MD} & =d-m \\  & =(-i+2j+k)-(-i-k) \\  & =2j+2k \\  & =⟨0,2,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{MA} & =a-m \\  & =(i-2j+k)-(-i-k) \\  & =2i-2j+2k \\  & =⟨2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{MD}\times \overset{\to }{MA} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(2\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot 2)i-(0\cdot 2-2\cdot 2)j+(0\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 2)k \\  & =8i+4j-4k \\  & =⟨8,4,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{MD}$ and $\overset{\to }{MA}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{MD}\times \overset{\to }{MA}| \\  & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{96} \\  & =4\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,DMA$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{4\sqrt{6}}{2}=2\sqrt{6}.
$$

Let's also compute $MA$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}MA & =|\overset{\to }{MA}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot MA,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot MA \\ 2\sqrt{6} & =\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\ 2\sqrt{6} & =DH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ DH & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ DH & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-103991:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)} & =\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+6},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
7=A(x+6)+B(x-1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-6,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(-6+6)+B(-6-1) \\ 7 & =-7B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(1+6)+B(1-1) \\ 7 & =7A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)} & =\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+6})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+6|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=1,b=-1,$ and $a+b=1-1=0.$

q-103989:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} & =\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x-4=A(x-4)+Bx.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(4)-4 & =A(4-4)+B(4) \\ 4 & =4B \\ 1 & =B\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-4 & =A(0-4)+B(0) \\ -4 & =-4A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} & =\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-68215:
Notice that as $x\to 0,$ both numerator and denominator approach $0.$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x}{3x}=\frac{0}{0},
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}=1
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x}{3x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}-\frac{x}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}-{lim}_{x\to 0}\,1] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (1-1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-73546:
First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1}{{\theta }^{2}} & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}{{\theta }^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}}\cdot {lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

- Consider the first limit. Notice that as $\theta \to 0,$ both numerator and denominator approach $0.$ 

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}}=\frac{0}{0},
$$

which is an indeterminate form. 

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}} & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\theta })}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\theta }]}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡0}=1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}}\cdot {lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } & =1\cdot 1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49902:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x}{(x-2)^{2}} & =\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{(x-2)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-2)^{2}$ and get

$$
4x=A(x-2)+B.
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2) & =A(2-2)+B \\ 8 & =0+B \\ B & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0) & =A(0-2)+B \\ 0 & =-2A+B \\ 0 & =-2A+8 \\ A & =\frac{8}{2} \\ A & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{4x}{(x-2)^{2}}=\frac{4}{(x-2)}+\frac{8}{(x-2)^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{4x}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3}^{4}(\frac{4}{(x-2)}+\frac{8}{(x-2)^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+8{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|{|}_{3}^{4}+8(-\frac{1}{x-2}){|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4-2|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-2|)+8(-\frac{1}{4-2}+\frac{1}{3-2}) \\  & =4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4-2|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-2|)+8(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2+4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-11373:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{14{x}^{2}+47x+42}{(2x+3)^{2}(x+3)}=\frac{A}{(2x+3)}+\frac{B}{(2x+3)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x+3)}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(2x+3)^{2}(x+3)$ and get

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(0)+1 & =A(0+1)^{2}+B(0+1)+C \\ 1 & =A+B-2 \\ A+B & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=-2$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-2)+1 & =A(-2+1)^{2}+B(-2+1)+C \\ -5 & =A-B-2 \\ A-B & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations $A-B=-3$ and $A+B=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =-3+3 \\ 2A & =0 \\ A & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting back into $A+B=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0+B & =3 \\ B & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{3x+1}{(x+1)^{3}}=\frac{3}{(x+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}}.

$$
